note: A beginner's first scale with no position number in it: the first step says what is on the neck (the notes of the minor pentatonic scale, each dot a note to play) and spells the run out string by string. Three sections change one thing each: every note, only the roots, then phrases that end on a root. It moves to other keys and tempos, so the key and tempo are written as params; the last line, opened with {{?key}}, carries what guitar-beginner-your-a-phrases-in-e (folded in) was for: a phrase is a shape, so it moves to another key whole.

exercise.title: {{=key}} minor pentatonic, then your own phrases
exercise.why: A phrase made from a minor pentatonic scale sounds finished when it lands on the root, so knowing where the three roots sit among the dots lets you make music from the start.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome at {{=bpm}}. Under it is the neck with the notes of the {{=key}} minor pentatonic scale: each dot is a note to play.
Start on the ringed {{1}} on the low E string and play both dots on that string. Then play both dots on each next string up to the high e string, and come back down the same way, one note per beat.
Practice until your fingers find the next dot without you looking.

Now only the three {{1}} notes are in play, and the other dots are faded. Tap a {{1}} on the neck below to hear it, then play it on your guitar, and hop between the three in any order.
Practice until you can find each one without looking.
{{?key}}In another key the dots sit on other frets, and the three roots keep their places among them.

Press Play below to start the backing track: drums and bass, a little faster than the metronome was. Make up short phrases from any of the dots and end each one on one of the ringed {{1}} notes. Leave a gap after each phrase.
Then end one phrase on another note and listen for how it sounds unfinished.
{{?key}}In another key a phrase you made keeps its shape: play it from the same dots on their new frets.
